Industry observers note that griffin Park was much beloved, of course, and its peculiar feature of boasting a pub at each of the four corners of the ground was part of the game’s folklore. But Brentford pulled off an architectural wonder with the Gtech, squeezing it into a parcel of land in the shadow of the raised section of the M4 in west London.

The club has frequently had one of the best home records in the Premier League since coming up in 2021, which is testimony not just to the excellence of the players and manager but to the tight confines of the ground and the atmosphere it creates.

Recent findings suggest that it is no surprise it is attracting supporters who previously considered themselves without an affiliation. It is the type of stadium, and club, that makes fans feel they belong.

Division: Championship Opened: 1801 Capacity: 10,500.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of Wrexham with distaste.

I went to a lot of games in Wrexham in the late 70s and early 80s. My best mate, Bryn, was from the town so when his mum and dad took him to visit family there, I went along and we headed for the Racecourse Ground.

I’m not one of those who regards the Ryan Reynolds/Rob McElhenney takeover of the club with distaste, although I am aware that my friend and colleague Ian Herbert, a Wrexham fan and a club scholar, has had some misgivings.

Nothing in football is ever quite as wholesome as it seems but so far, it feels as if it has been good for the club and for the town.

Sources indicate that I don’t know what their long-term motives are but they have poured a lot of money into the team and into the infrastructure, and the club has risen and risen through the leagues. It’s bringing more light into a community that has had its share of hard times.

I was at the Racecourse, by the way, when Mark Hughes scored his spectacular overhead kick against Spain in 1985. It’s still one of the top five goals I’ve ever seen live.

(The others: Angel Di Maria for Argentina at the Lusail Stadium in the 2022 World Cup final, Zlatan Ibrahimovic for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in 2012, Dennis Bergkamp for the Netherlands against Argentina at the Stade Velodrome at France '98 and Norman Whiteside for Manchester United against Everton at Wembley in the 1985 FA Cup final).

21. St Andrew's, Birmingham City.

Division: Championship Opened: 1906 Capacity: 29,409.

There are wealthy owners at Birmingham now, of course, and massive plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Down the winding stairs from the press box, though the main reception area where staff are trying to sort ticket requests, through the foyer, down another set of steps and into a tunnel below the Main Stand where four garden forks hang on the wall outside the groundsman’s room – St Andrew’s is still a beautiful stadium that mixes old-school elements and modern stands.

It’s a great place to watch a game. If it gets overshadowed by Aston Villa and West Brom, it still feels as if the soul of the Second City is alive in this place.

There are wealthy owners now, of course, and substantial plans, but St Andrew’s is still at the heart of everything.

Industry observers note that 20. Stadium of Light, Sunderland.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1997 Capacity: 48,095.

Sunderland have some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

According to recent reports, I loved Roker Park. Like Maine Road, I’d have it in my top 10 grounds if Sunderland were still playing there now and I feel lucky to have stood in the away end there and been treated to the full force of the Roker Roar.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve never been quite sure what to make of its successor, the Stadium of Light. I’m not even sure about the name, which is dramatic, certainly, but is also an obvious copy of the original Benfica ground in Lisbon – which opened in 1954 and held 130,000 at its peak.

Sources indicate that the design is rather uninspiring for such an evocative name, too. It’s uncomfortably close to identikit latest-build, but I have friends who say it’s their favourite anywhere.

The stadium does sit proudly atop the bluffs of the River Wear and it’s wonderful to see the team on the up again and back in the Premier League. These are some of the best supporters in the country and the noise the fans make when the biggest occasions present themselves is up there with anyone.

Recent findings suggest that 19. Bramall Lane, Sheffield United.

Division: Championship Opened: 1855 Capacity: 32,050.

Bramall Lane's Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Bramall Lane is still the only ground where I’ve sat in the dugout during a league game.

Recent findings suggest that neil Warnock is a friend of mine and when he was in charge at Sheffield United, he let me sit next to him in an end-of-season Championship game against Ipswich Town. I got a front row seat for Rob Kozluk, one of the game’s great sledgers, doing his best to wind up then-Ipswich boss Joe Royle.

According to recent reports, I can’t think of many better grounds to have had the privilege. Bramall Lane is a cauldron of noise, full of history and passion, in the heart of the city.

Its Kop singing the Greasy Chip Butty song is one of the iconic experiences in English football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1877 Capacity: 40,044.

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

All stadiums change and modernise with the years but there are few stadiums which have changed as dramatically as Stamford Bridge.

It was once an intimidating place, dominated by the Shed, a sprawling, boisterous semi-circular terrace behind one of the goals that was synonymous with the crowd problems of the 1970s and early 80s.

Going to watch a Chelsea game now is an entirely different experience. The transformation began under Ken Bates, one of a group of visionary businessmen who changed the way we watch football, and then continued under Roman Abramovich.

And now, for many, going to Chelsea, with its towering West Stand and opulent corporate boxes, is a boutique experience not out of place with the hugely affluent area in which it stands.

Sources indicate that you can still feel the history of the place when you visit, though. To its credit, the club preserved the original wall that stood at the back of the Shed and it remains in place, used to display pictures of Chelsea legends.

Maybe I should declare a certain bias here, too: the food in the press room at the Bridge is the best in the Premier League.

Sources indicate that 17. Selhurst Park, Crystal Palace.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1924 Capacity: 25,194.

A trip to Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park is one of the best experiences in the English game.

In a recent development, I used to be put off by what I saw, pathetically, as the difficulty of getting to Selhurst Park in south London. Difficult to drive to, hard to find a parking space, not on the Tube, etc, etc.

It has been revealed that I got over that some time ago. A trip to Palace is one of the best experiences in the English game.

The atmosphere generated by the Holmesdale Road stand, in particular, makes Selhurst Park one of the best grounds in England to watch football.

Sources indicate that other clubs have seen the volume of their support dim as the demographic of their fans has changed but that has not happened at Selhurst Park. It is one of the few places left that has the power to intimidate and it is all the better for that.

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

One of the great surviving community grounds, a beautiful, steep-sided gem of a boutique stadium in Shepherd’s Bush, Loftus Road is a place to cherish.

When Bernie Ecclestone was a part-owner of the club, I sat in the directors’ box with him a few times and got shushed by Flavio Briatore for talking too much when my neighbour kept asking me questions. That may have been the first time anybody has ever been accused of talking more than Flavio.

The football wasn’t the best during their time there but the hospitality was: they had Mayfair restaurant Cipriani doing the catering.

They are long gone now but the stadium still remains, a wonderful anachronism in a changing world.

Industry observers note that 15. City Ground, Nottingham Forest.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1898 Capacity: 30,404.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special - take Nottingham Forest's City Ground for example.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special.

It has been revealed that my favourite was always the walk through Queens Gardens in Perth to the WACA. The stroll down from the city centre to the Adelaide Oval is beautiful, too, and the walk along the Thames to Craven Cottage is part of what makes that ground special.

It’s the same with the City Ground. I always park in the same spot, near the River Trent, and walk along the river path until you can see the Forest fans streaming down towards the entrances at the Trent End.

When you get closer, you see the majesty of Trent Bridge next to the City Ground, too, and you feel you’re right at the heart of British sport.

There’s so much history at the City Ground, so much achievement, so much tradition and such a stunning location. It’s a wonderful place to watch a game.

Division: League One Opened: 1901 Capacity: 17,904.

Home Park in Plymouth is one of the best football experiences in the league.

My affection for Home Park was well entrenched even before I took my seat in the lovely Mayflower Grandstand and watched one of the greatest FA Cup shocks of recent years unfold there in February 2025 when the Pilgrims beat Liverpool.

That was a day to cherish everything about Home Park and the Green Army and the proud local identity enshrined there.

The Mayflower Grandstand, which was renovated recently, remains a beautiful piece of stadium architecture, the staff and stewards are uniformly friendly and welcoming, and the ground occupies a handsome spot in a park on a hill not too far from Plymouth Hoe.

It’s one of the best football experiences in England.

13. Prenton Park, Tranmere Rovers.

Division: League Two Opened: 1912 Capacity: 15,012.

Tranmere Rovers' Prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while.

Prenton Park became a beloved second home for me for a while. Like Stockport, they used to play their home games on a Friday night for a time and that offered a chance to go and watch them under the lights.

It has been revealed that I loved Prenton Park and its sense of community and its noble old stands from the start. When I started work as a trainee on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo in the early 90s, I got to cover Tranmere in the glory days under Johnny King when John Aldridge, who had returned from Real Sociedad, was scoring for fun.

The atmosphere inside the ground on some of those nights on the Wirral was electric. When I was a news reporter at the Echo, I even had to go round to the house of Tranmere’s midfielder Kenny Irons in Norris Green to check out a story.

Kenny had been playing football in his front garden and kicked a ball over a hedge into next door’s garden. His neighbour was an old lady and she wouldn’t give Kenny his ball back. When I pitched up on his doorstep, he saw the funny side.

12. Wham Stadium, Accrington Stanley.

Division: League Two Opened: 1968 Capacity: 5,278.

The Wham Stadium has improved out of all recognition since Andy Holt became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a community.

For once, I can turn a blind eye to the renaming of the ground as the Wham Stadium.

That’s because I know how much love and commitment and time and money the Stanley owner, Andy Holt, has put into the resurrection of his local team since he cleared its debts in 2015 when it was on the brink of folding.

According to recent reports, andy doesn’t get much thanks for it and continues to fund the club to the tune of £250,000 a year, despite having claimed he would step down last year. When he does, he will bequeath a lasting legacy in this part of Lancashire.

Industry observers note that the ground has improved out of all recognition since he became involved and any visit to it is a visit to the heart of the difference one man can make to a football club and a community. Visionaries like Andy are few and far between in football and the game will be poorer for his absence.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 43,205 (temporarily reduced to 36,887).

Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game, a ground dripping with history.

Once one of the great architectural jewels of the English game, Villa Park lost the beauty of Archibald Leitch’s magnificent original Trinity Road Stand in 2000 when it was demolished.

Its loss was a sign of how shabbily we treat the idea of protecting our football heritage in this country.

It has been revealed that despite that, Villa Park remains one of the great arenas in the English game. I stood on the old Holte End in 1983 to see Villa, then European Cup holders, play the mighty Juventus. In October 2024 I was there again when Unai Emery’s side beat Bayern Munich, the team they conquered in the 1982 European Cup final, in their home return to the Champions League.

The atmosphere that night, with the Holte End in full voice, was a wonderful reminder of the great occasions of the past at a ground that feels like stadium aristocracy.

Sources indicate that 10. Old Trafford, Manchester United.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 74,244.

Old Trafford's iconic Holy Trinity statue stands guard on the forecourt outside the stadium.

Old Trafford is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs and memorable nights.

Industry observers note that yes, the roof leaks and, yes, Old Trafford could do with a bit of love and attention but there is a magic about this stadium that can never fade. (At least not until Sir Jim Ratcliffe knocks it down and builds the 100,000-seat tourist attraction that is his vision of the football of the future).

Recent findings suggest that much of that comes from the glories it has witnessed. Sit in the Stretford End and gaze down at a pitch where Duncan Edwards once strode across the turf, George Best danced through the mud and where Bobby Charlton and Denis Law and Bryan Robson and Roy Keane and Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney have played.

It has been revealed that it is still a magnificent stadium, redolent of so many triumphs. Outside, on the forecourt, the Holy Trinity statue, a tribute to Best, Charlton and Law, is a place of pilgrimage. As is the Munich Clock, a poignant reminder of the loss of so many of the Busby Babes in 1958.

I was standing on the terraces there when United beat Diego Maradona’s Barcelona 3-0 in the Cup Winners’ Cup in March 1984 and it was one of the best atmospheres I’ve ever felt at an English league ground.

It’s a wonderful place, one of the stadiums that can lay claim to nurturing a chunk of the heart of the English game. They just need a team to be worthy of it again.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1897 Capacity: 37,645.

It has been revealed that I love Leeds United's Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

I love Elland Road. Even before I get into the ground, I love Elland Road.

The statue of Billy Bremner, which is usually festooned with scarves and surrounded by tributes to Leeds fans who have passed away, should be a starting point for any visit.

At the other end of the emotional spectrum, fish and chip shops are a decent component of a matchday experience and Graveley's, on Elland Road itself, which has a long queue snaking up to its door from two hours before kick-off, is one of the best football chippies in the country.

The stadium is a proper cathedral of our game, too. One-club cities sometimes generate that kind of passion and it’s evident at Elland Road. I like the fact the stands are named after Don Revie, Norman Hunter, Jack Charlton and John Charles, not an IT tech giant or an airline or a waste management service.

And I love the singing of Marching On Together, a club anthem that dates back more than 50 years, not one of the manufactured club songs you hear at some stadiums these days that mark a cosmetic attempt at authenticity.

Recent findings suggest that you feel the heat of English football at Elland Road, you feel the intensity of it and what it means. At a lot of substantial clubs, that feeling has been lost. But it's alive here.

8. St James' Park, Newcastle United.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1892 Capacity: 52,719.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

In a recent development, newcastle are leaning towards building a new stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Every time I arrive in the city and see St James’ staring down from its vantage point above it, it sends shivers down my spine.

In a recent development, its position is a symbol of its importance to the city. Inside, it generates one of the best atmospheres in the country, its fans are among the most loyal and the Gallowgate End is one of the most revered sections in our football history.

Newcastle are leaning towards building a fresh stadium adjacent to the current site and moving to that. Please don’t.

7. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Tottenham Hotspur.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2019 Capacity: 62,850.

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other new-builds lack.

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the fresh stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone.

My favourite upcoming stadium anywhere is RB Leipzig’s Red Bull Stadion because of the way it was constructed inside the bowl of the old Zentralstadion but in England, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium stand out.

There is an ambition about Spurs' stadium that so many other fresh-builds lack, particularly the steepling end behind one of the goals that is said to be modelled on the Yellow Wall at the Westfalenstadion in Dortmund.

I love the nods to the club’s history, particularly the replica of the cockerel that sits above the South Stand and the black and white photos that line the corridors outside the press room.

Former Spurs chairman Daniel Levy got plenty of criticism for the failures of the club on the pitch but the newly introduced stadium still stands as his stunning legacy even now that he has gone.

Industry observers note that 6. Cherry Red Records Stadium, AFC Wimbledon.

Division: League One Opened: 2020 Capacity: 9,150.

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football.

I never made it to the old Wimbledon ground at Plough Lane, which is a regret, but I had one of the best of football days when I finally made it to the Cherry Red Records Stadium, near to the site of the old ground, when they played the team that nearly drove them into oblivion, MK Dons, in September 2024.

Just setting foot in this stadium is to feel what it is like to support a team that is at the heart of its community and to be among a fanbase whose team means more to it than just wins and losses.

Love for the game and the team and reverence for the history of the club, the club that was stolen from them and the club they rebuilt, is everywhere, from the kitsch statue of Dave Beasant at the front of the stadium to the illustration on the walls.

It feels like a stadium where everybody knows each other, like neighbours in a street, like a giant, loving, proud family that refuses to be torn apart. The beauty of the architecture here is not in the stadium buildings. It is in the knowledge that this is something built by fans.

If I lived in London, and Stockport weren't playing, this is where I’d watch my football.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1896 Capacity: 27,782.

Craven Cottage, home of Fulham, is one of the jewels of English football heritage.

Craven Cottage is one of the jewels of English football heritage, and Fulham’s stadium on the banks of the Thames has achieved the difficult task of modernising the ground without losing its character.

The presence of the Cottage, the most glorious eccentricity remaining in our 92 stadiums, in one corner of the ground, is central to that, of course, and helps to make watching a match there so special.

This is a club that has taken care to preserve its history and value a stadium that is different.

Even the walk to the ground through Bishop’s Park and along the path by the river, adds to the pleasure of the experience. It is a joy to visit.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 8,714.

Exeter City have been owned by their supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, they are a shining example of how successful the model can be.

I was there last year to see Stockport County play and every away fan got a voucher offering a free cup of tea.

It was the summer of 2010 when Exeter City forward Adam Stansfield died of cancer at the age of 31.

‘Stanno’, the father of current Birmingham striker Jay Stansfield, was a hero at the beautiful St James Park stadium, nestled in a nook at the foot of a steep hill and bordered by neat, densely packed terraced streets and a railway cutting.

I drove down there with my elder daughter to look at the tributes to Stansfield and we wandered among the bouquets of flowers and the keepsakes left by heartbroken young fans and the emotional messages that had been left in their thousands on the Big Bank.

It was impossible not to be moved by the profound emotional connection between a city and its club and as the years have passed, St James Park has come to embody for me everything that a football ground should be: full of character and care and camaraderie and community and passion and pride in what it stands for.

I was there last year to see Stockport play and there was a note next to the away turnstile – a turnstile made in another age at the Albion Works in Patricroft – saying: ‘Hatters Fans: Thank you for travelling 474 miles to support your club today.’.

Industry observers note that every away fan also got a voucher offering a free cup of tea. The club has been owned by its supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, it is a model of how successful it can be.

Sources indicate that the Big Bank has been extended and is now the biggest terrace in English football. So the locals tell me, anyway. There is a club museum, a stall selling farm produce and a supporters’ club bar with big screens.

They built a new stand a few years back, too. It’s called the Adam Stansfield Stand.

According to recent reports, 3. Hill Dickinson Stadium, Everton.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2025 Capacity: 52,769.

If you are going to move to a new ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium.

I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

I loved Goodison Park and I hated the idea of Everton moving from it. I understand, too, the attitude of some Evertonians who feel the identity of the club will be forever twinned with Goodison.

According to recent reports, but if you are going to move to a upcoming ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium. I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

I loved everything about it, from its setting on the banks of Mersey, at the heart of the city’s dock culture, which is such a critical component of Liverpool’s heritage, to its vertiginous stands and its community feel.

It has been revealed that it still feels like Everton. It doesn’t feel as if the club has been deracinated by its move, as West Ham have been by the change to the London Stadium. Everton now have a stadium that is one of the city’s great landmarks, the first thing visitors to the city see when they sail in on the cruise ships that arrive in Liverpool from all over the world.

Sources indicate that next to the stadium, there still stands the careworn edifice of Victoria Tower, the famous hexagonal clocktower also known as the Dockers’ Clock, that cruise ship passengers used to set their watches to when they arrived from the USA in the city’s boom times. Everton’s home stands proudly beside it now, a symbol of a fresh Merseyside.

Even more than the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Everton's ground is a standard-bearer for the newly introduced generation of English stadiums.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 61,726.

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing thanks to fearsome tales about The Kop.

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't then and it isn’t now.

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing.

The tales of The Kop and what they would do to you if they heard your accent were fearsome and when I finally plucked up the courage to go and watch Manchester United play there, I bought a ticket among the home fans and did not speak a word for more than two hours.

According to recent reports, but that didn’t stop me being in awe of the place when I first visited. I have never been anywhere like it for the passion and the noise it generated.

Yes, maybe its atmosphere has been slightly diluted by the owners' attempts to attract a newly introduced, high-yield breed of casual fan but the ferocity of the emotion the place can still muster can be incredibly moving.

The 2005 Champions League semi-final second leg against Chelsea was probably the noisiest and the most spine-tingling I’ve ever witnessed it although the tie against Barcelona, at the same stage of the competition in 2019, is seared on my brain for similar reasons.

In a recent development, A love for a stadium is about memories, too. My first jobs in journalism were on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo and I spent many wide-eyed afternoons in the old press box at Anfield and in the press conferences afterwards, listening to Kenny Dalglish and, later, Graeme Souness, two of the best British footballers who have ever lived.

Industry observers note that once, on my first visit to the press box, I made the mistake of sitting in Tommy Smith’s seat and was suddenly aware of the hulking presence of the Anfield Iron looming silently above me and a colleague telling me to get up sharpish. I never sat in that seat again.

Industry observers note that some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't and it isn’t. Corporate incursions have altered it but it still has the power to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end.

It has been revealed that 1. Edgeley Park, Stockport County.

Division: League One Opened: 1891 Capacity: 10,800.

I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for Stockport. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

Recent findings suggest that my family didn’t have any history with Stockport County. I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for them. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

But he was from Heaton Chapel and his grandfather made, and lost, a fortune in the hatting industry in the town in the late 19th century, and he was fiercely proud of Stockport Viaduct and its history and he took me to my first game at Edgeley Park on Monday, April 9, 1979.

We sat in Block A of the Main Stand, now the Danny Bergara Stand, and I breathed in the smell of cigar smoke that drifted up from the man in the sheepskin jacket sitting a couple of rows in front of us and thrilled at the noise coming from the terraces opposite and gazed up to my left at the men working away on their typewriters in the press box, men whose faces I recognised because I had seen their photo bylines in the Manchester Evening News.

I have mentioned elsewhere the curious wonder I felt when people who were strangers to me greeted my dad by name as we walked up the steps to our seats.

I didn’t think my dad had ever been to Edgeley Park before but these people knew him anyway because they were from Stockport and he was from Stockport and those moments made me realise for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community. Not for everyone, but for some of us.

And so even if he wasn’t a fan, I still feel connected to my dad every time I use one of my season tickets, that I bought in a row next to the press box, and gaze over at the place we sat that first time.

I am not a proper fan like the supporters who go week in and week out but I love that ground. I am not a member of any London clubs but Edgeley Park is my club and now, just like my dad, I know people when I go.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

Edgeley Park was where I realised for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community.

I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

Mark Stott has not just invested in the first team and dragged County back up into the Football League but he has bought a fresh training ground and lavished a lot of love on upgrading facilities for fans in the Cheadle End.

The Danny Bergara Stand still oozes character, it is still similar to the way I remember it from that first game in 1979 and much of the rest of the stadium has been renovated and improved.

I haven’t been so much in recent seasons because I've been spending my spare weekends trying to complete my 92.

Industry observers note that I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • "It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.
  • Sources indicate that earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defense Committee.
  • "The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius remarked, announcing an action blueprint to address the issue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"It was clear to us from the outset that the analysis would uncover uncomfortable truths," Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) told theBundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.

Sources indicate that earlier that day, he had presented the findings of the Bundeswehr's first study into unreported cases of sexual misconduct to the Defense Committee. According to the findings, sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr is far more widespread than previously known.

"The study has shown that only between one third and one sixth of cases are reported," Pistorius remarked, announcing an action blueprint to address the issue.

In a recent development, "There is zero tolerance for sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr. This is nothing less than a matter of upholding the human dignity enshrined in our Basic Law. And that principle applies all the more within the Bundeswehr.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the study examined incidents that had gone unreported, the so-called "dark figure" of cases that never reach official statistics. The Bundeswehr Centre of Military History and Social Sciences (ZMSBw) surveyed 45,000 service members, around 18% of whom responded. More than 8,100 questionnaires were evaluated and supplemented with individual and group interviews. According to the institute, the data are statistically representative.

According to the study, younger women in the lower ranks are particularly affected by sexual misconduct. Among men, non-heterosexual soldiers are disproportionately affected. The perpetrators are predominantly male. Statistically, combat units do not differ from the rest of the armed forces.

Female service members in units with a higher proportion of women (more than 15%) are less likely to be affected.

Verbal harassment is by far the most common form of misconduct, according to the study. Around 72% of female soldiers and 31% of male soldiers stated they had experienced verbal harassment at least once during their military service. In the 12 months preceding the survey, 38% of female soldiers and 16% of male soldiers reported experiencing verbal sexual harassment.

For physical harassment, 9% of female soldiers and 3% of male soldiers reported incidents of physical sexual misconduct, and 2% of both women and men stated they had experienced sexual violence.

The study also examined why service members chose not to report incidents. The most commonly cited reason was not wanting to draw attention to themselves.

"There appears to be a lack of awareness of the reporting channels. And, for me, the decisive concern is trust in those channels," Pistorius concluded.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that in response, the Bundeswehr aims to improve awareness of how and where cases of sexual harassment can be reported. That is precisely where the environmentalist Greens, who are in opposition in the Bundestag, direct their criticism.

Defense policy spokesperson Sara Nanni is calling for "an external reporting office, alongside the regular disciplinary process, with investigative powers and the authority to take disciplinary action where appropriate." Such an independent point of contact, she argues, is needed in cases where superiors within the Bundeswehr fail to fulfill their responsibilities.

It has been revealed that another consequence of the study is the expansion of support services for those affected. A counseling center established in early November will soon be available around the clock. Supervisors are also to receive enhanced awareness training and improved instruction.

"Sexual misconduct will become part of training at every level, from the very beginning," noted Bundeswehr Inspector General Carsten Breuer.

In addition, the way supervisors handle reported cases will become a standing criterion in their performance evaluations. "Anyone who fails to lead by example, tolerates misconduct, or does not address it consistently will no longer hold a leadership position," Defense Minister Pistorius stressed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the study was prompted by a growing number of reports of sexual misconduct received by former Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces Eva Högl. Most of those who approached her were female soldiers. Högl called for the study into unreported cases in 2024. The process gained further momentum following incidents at the Parachute Regiment in Zweibrücken that came to light at the beginning of this year and also involved allegations of sexual misconduct.

In a recent development, the current Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces, Henning Otte, described the figures revealed by the study as "dramatically high." The findings had also made it clear, he noted, "that there is a lack of trust in the Bundeswehr's structures. The Ministry of Defense must now take this study seriously and translate its findings into a leadership culture that is truly lived in practice.".

According to recent reports, the Bundeswehr urgently needs additional personnel and has been actively recruiting women. However, the study's findings are unlikely to make attracting more female recruits any easier. Women remain significantly underrepresented across nearly all branches of the armed forces.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Antonio Conte insists he would love ‘before ending my career to take over a club that is already organised’ after years of ‘building value’ from troubled situations like Juventus, Chelsea, Inter and Napoli.

The coach is presently between jobs after walking away from Napoli in two years where he won the Serie A title and the Supercoppa Italiana.

There were reports he could come to Manchester United or even return to his old side Juve, but he is in no rush for his next role.

Speaking to the Cronache di Spogliatoio podcast, Conte did outline his greatest strength, and why he perhaps eager to cast it aside and do something different next time.

“There is one thing I’d love to do before ending my career as a coach, which is to take over a club that is already organised,” stated Conte.

“It would be like stepping into a Formula 1 car in pole position. It never happened in my career, but evidently that is just the way it goes for me. I always arrived at complicated situations and was fortunate, but also deserve credit, for taking a team back to victory.

“Often, it involved returning them to their history, a dimension that perhaps they had forgotten.”.

It all sounds like the scenario at Manchester United, who have not won the Premier League since 2013, following in the footsteps of other clubs he went through.

“It happened at Juventus, who got back to winning after seven years, Inter hadn’t won the Scudetto for 10, and Chelsea were coming off a disastrous season when I arrived, finishing in 10th place, but then won the Premier League with me.

“The same was true at Napoli, where they had finished 10th, then I arrived and took them to victory.”.

That also means Conte brings with him certain expectations, something he is quick to point out in press conferences from the very start.

“It is inevitable that when you arrive with a curriculum like this, you are accompanied by major expectations. People and the media expect you to win. I still remember when I arrived at Napoli, a team that finished 10th, a beautiful city, their objective was to qualify for the Champions League.

“I thought I could just enjoy my work and the city for a while, but the moment I signed, the media completely changed the message. I don’t know how many other coaches would be treated that way.”.

In fairness, Napoli had won the Scudetto the previous season under Luciano Spalletti, then limped to 10th place after going through a series of coaches, but retained much the same team.

When it comes to Inter, Conte also argues he laid the foundations for all those who followed him.

“I arrived and the Appiano Gentile ground was disastrous, the pitches had significant holes in, there was always an alibi from the staff. Inter invested in revamping the pitch, and a month later it was ruined again,” said the coach.

“The club spent €120,000 and in those two years, I also asked for them to set up somewhere to sleep. If you look at the Inter training ground today, it is a gem.

“There are many clubs where there is a before me, and an after me, and those who come later find this.”.

Conte also discussed the player sales that sides like Inter made thanks to his development of certain players.

Sources indicate that “I become an investment for clubs that pays off. We signed Romelu Lukaku and Achraf Hakimi, then sold them on for €120m to Chelsea and €70m to PSG. I added value to the squad.”.

Recent findings suggest that "Kevin is the only wee anomaly. We didn't get him back from Russia on Wednesday night because of a few complications with transport, but we managed to get him back in at lunchtime on Thursday," McInnes said.

Rangers face Motherwell in Lanarkshire on Saturday and have a solid away record - but dropped points in two away draws prior to the win at St Mirren.

McInnes is expecting a stiff test as he believes the Steelmen are beginning to perform like the side that impressed throughout last season and qualified for Europe.

"I think they have got a lot of traits and similarities to the team that got a lot of success last year. I think over the last two or three games they've started to look a wee bit more like that," he added.

"They'll be a difficult opponent, but if we want to get to where we want to get to this season, we want to make sure we leave Motherwell with all three points.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham will watch Stade de Reims star Yaya Fofana in action this weekend ahead of a possible transfer move, according to French outlet Foot Mercato.

Fofana has enjoyed a remarkable season for the Ligue 2 side and he will undoubtedly feature heavily in the headlines over the coming weeks following his goalscoring exploits as the January transfer window edges ever closer.

A versatile midfielder capable of playing in a number of positions, Fofana, who was recently called up to the Ivory Coast squad for the first time, has been utilised as an attacking midfielder by Reims boss Nicolas Usai this term and that has resulted in a real purple patch in front of goal.

Fofana has ten goals and three assists to his name from his 12 appearances this season, including nine goals in his last eight league games for his club side.

His form in the final third has come to the attention of Tottenham, with Foot Mercato reporting that the north London club will have people in the stands to watch the 22-year-old in action against St-Etienne on Saturday evening.

The French outlet report that Reims do not want to see their player leave during the January transfer window.

However, a permanent move with a six-month loan move back to Les rouges et blancs for the remainder of the season could well work for all parties concerned.

It is believed that a transfer away for Fofana would have to be in excess of the €25m (£21m) they recently received for Patrick Zabi following his move to Paris FC in the summer.

Yaya Fofana's 2026/27 season in numbers.

So what exactly would Fofana bring to Tottenham?

Well, Roberto De Zerbi would certainly be inheriting a very talented player and one that can play in a number of positions.

Fofana's ability to play further forward and flourish in the final third has been evident this season after so far amassing ten goals in 12 league appearances for Reims.

"Yaya is an instinctive player, so you have to give him a lot of freedom," stated Usai, as reported by Morning Foot.

"He is able to play in a double pivot in the fairly low middle, he is able to play playmaker, he is able to play attacker, he is able to play on one side.".

He added: "It's a talented player, but I insist that it's really an instinctive profile, so he must be left free.

"Of course he has defensive instructions and that he must tune defensively in the service of the collective, but when he has the ball or when he is able to dezone, the partners simply need to be able to adjust their movement.".

It has been revealed that on the prospect of losing his player in January, Usai stated: "No, no, no fear. Really, it's early November, so I don't ask myself that kind of question.".

Luxury automaker Mercedes-Benz is halting investment at its facilities in Germany, a board members confirmed on Thursday.

Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger mentioned in an interview published on the company's intranet.

Germany's major IG Metall trade union has enabled the possibility of longer warning strikes amid difficult negotiations for industrial employees.

"The board of IG Metall has pave the way for 24-hour warning strikes in the metalworking and electrical industry," the union said on Thursday.

The union accuses employers of intransigence after three rounds of negotiations without clear progress.

On Wednesday, regional chapters appealed for authorization for full-day warning strikes — the last step before a full union vote and an indefinite labor dispute.

Recent findings suggest that "This escalation is completely excessive and counterproductive," Udo Dinglreiter, the president of the employers' umbrella organization, Gesamtmetall, said. He said that hundreds of thousands of jobs could be at risk.

IG Metall's first chairperson Christiane Benner countered that "the employers want to turn this round of collective bargaining into a dispute over principles." Another union official remarked they were offering what amounted to a real-terms pay cut rather than seeking solutions.

IG Metall is calling for a 5% pay increase and other improved conditions for some 3.7 million workers starting in November, while employers have offered a one-off payment in 2027 coupled with a 1.3% increase starting in the summer of 2028.

The union estimates that around 464,000 employees took part in the initial wave of warning strikes that were limited to periods of hours, rather than full days.

Employers argue that they're treading a difficult line between trying not to cut jobs and meeting calls for improved pay amid widespread industrial sector layoffs in Germany in recent years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, 'Tis the season, already. Preparations are underway around Germany and in several cities, Christmas markets are opening to the public.

Some markets are already open in Essen and in Hamburg, Duisburg's opens on Thursday, and Cologne's follows a day later.

The coupons.de website has sought to track the planned prices for mulled wine or Glühwein as the markets open their doors nationwide.

According to recent reports, the bad news? These prices are rising like so many others. The better news? The year-on-year increase is actually smaller than overall inflation figures, at around 1%.

In a recent development, on average, a cup is liable to set you back around €4.60 (roughly $5.10). Not entirely surprisingly, Munich tops the nationwide pricing chart, with the price peaking at €7. Other sites nationwide tend not to have the gall even to charge 6 euros.

Bargain hunters determined to get the best value mulled wine will need to venture deep into the center of Germany — hardly its core tourist hub — to find the lowest prices starting at around €3.50.

Deposits for the cup, the "Pfand," are also only going in one direction, and in the meantime range from €1 all the way up to €5. But there's a strong argument, particularly with the better designs or after a memorable trip, that this can be money well spent as a memento!

Police in the Emsland region in the northwest near the border to the Netherlands have reported a major fire in a complex of residential and commercial buildings in Papenburg.

The fire broke out on Wednesday afternoon, police mentioned the following morning, causing damages worth "at least €10 million ($11 million)." Several hundred emergency services personnel were deployed.

"Based on current findings, the fire broke out in the sauna area of a gym facility on site, and quickly spread to further parts of the complex of buildings," police wrote.

Two men were in the sauna at the time and initially tried to douse the flames but without success.

Police mentioned the buildings were evacuated as the fire spread, with some surrounding buildings also being cleared as a precaution because of possible smoke-related dangers.

Sources indicate that several people were injured, police said, including the two men in the sauna area suffering mild burns and suspected smoke inhalation sickness. They were treated in a nearby hospital but soon discharged.

In a recent development, "There were also injuries among the first responders," police wrote. "Four police officers, two firefighters and members of the rescue teams suffered mild injuries, particularly via smoke inhalation.".

Sources indicate that the fire was only extinguished late on Wednesday night, several hours after it started. The area is sealed off, with possible risks of damaged buildings collapsing. Police have also launched investigations into the fire's cause, but said that at present, the area was not safe for that work to start at full scale.

Germany's largest credit bureau Creditreform has published its "2026 Debtors' Atlas.".

According to recent reports, it finds that 10.16% of German adults, or 7.36 million people, exhibit at least the early warning signs of excessive debt. A year ago the ratio was 9.74%.

"The financial situation of private consumers has further deteriorated," Patrik-Ludwig Hantzsch, Creditreform's head of economic research, remarked. "In particular, the sharply increased living costs, energy costs and housing costs are straining expenditures.".

Hantzsch noted employment was also becoming an glitch once more, saying "above all, well-paid jobs in manufacturing industries have been cut back in large numbers in recent months.".

The report also highlights rising cases of signs of excessive debt prior to legal action being taken, such as payment reminders or warnings being sent, saying "consumers are taking on more credit-financed expenditures — increasingly also for smaller purchases — at simultaneously rising interest rates.".

A larger share of men than women have excessive debts, perpetuating a longstanding trend.

People around the middle of their working lives, aged 30-39 and 40-49, are most likely to be affected — but the cohort with the fastest-rising share of people with excessive debts are young adults below the age of 30.

Bremen, Berlin, Saxony-Anhalt and North Rhine-Westphalia were among the states with the highest rates of excess debts, while the wealthy and fiscally conservative states of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg had the lowest levels.

Germany's main DAX stock market index has cleared the 27,000-point mark for the first time in its history in morning trading.

It climbed by around 1.3% in order to pass the milestone.

A combination of some positive outlook data from major companies, not least engineering giant Siemens, and the falling oil prices of recent days have helped fuel the uptick.

Siemens' shares had risen by almost 5%, to just over €291 (around $323) each, helping to spur on the gains and making the company the morning's top performer.

Despite several years of low growth and recession in the German economy, the DAX, like many Western indices, is now trading twice as high as it was prior to the COVID pandemic.

Hundreds of police officers searched apartments and meeting sites for the biker group "Gremium MC" in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg early on Thursday.

The state interior ministry remarked the operation was part of a move to outlaw three sub-chapters of the group, the ones based in Böblingen and Leonberg, as well as the "Gremium MC Chapter Nomads Bosphorus Türkiye.".

Recent findings suggest that this last group was highlighted as a meaningful part of Gremium MC by security officials. It describes itself on Facebook as a great example that "people of different cultures and faiths can be strong together," featuring images of men posing with knives and other weapons.

Gremium MC prominently incorporates into its iconography the symbol of the Prussian military medal for exceptional valor, the Iron Cross, which was discontinued after World War I, reintroduced by Adolf Hitler during World War II, and then scrapped for good.

State Interior Minister Manuel Hagel was expected to make further comments later in the day in Ludwigsburg.

Gremium MC is deemed an "outlaw motorcycle gang" in Baden-Württemberg's latest security report, a term used for biker groups that do not recognize the state monopoly on the use of force and are often tied to organized crime.

"Extortion, drug dealing and pimping in particular tend to be part of their activities," state authorities say.

Baden-Württemberg counts 154 biker chapters in the state with around 2,000 members.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 1972 in Mannheim, various chapters of Gremium MC across the country have faced legal issues in recent years. In 2021, another chapter in the southwest, Gremium MC Southgate in Heidelberg, was outlawed on suspicion of organized crime activity.

Police in Hanover reported early on Thursday that three men were injured by an unknown driver in a car in the nearby town of Ronneberg.

One person sustained severe injuries in the incident late on Wednesday, police said.

Two of the wounded were taken to a nearby hospital while the other could be cared for at the scene.

According to recent reports, police said the driver fled the scene and that a search operation was ongoing. Authorities were also still investigating a potential motive for the apparent attack.

Today's updates start with a focus between the southwestern Kurpfalz and Swabian regions, where police have launched major morning raids against a biker gang.

It has been revealed that the state Interior Ministry in Baden Württemberg has outlawed three of its chapters. Hundreds of police officers mobilized in the early hours of the morning.

The major IG Metall trade union is planning further strikes in the carmaking sector and other metalworking industries, with an announcement anticipated later in the day.

To the north, near Hanover, police report an apparent car attack injuring three men overnight.

Recent findings suggest that and in the spirit of offering the public service journalism people are truly thirsting for, we'll have some info on the average and localized pricing of mulled wine or Glühwein at Christmas markets this year, as the early birds start to open their doors to visitors. (Yes, already!).

Stay tuned for updates on all this and anything else of note in or pertaining to Germany as the day progresses.

Former Manchester City, Torino and England goalkeeper Hart has also used his column on the official City website to heap praise upon the Italian, who only recently won the Champions League at Paris Saint-Germain.

Donnarumma also won the Yashin Trophy, the goalkeeper’s equivalent of the Ballon d’Or, twice.

In a recent development, “I think some of Gianluigi’s performances were breathtaking, absolutely astonishing. He’s the captain of Italy. Simply put, he’s at the top table of goalkeepers,” wrote Hart.

Sources indicate that “I think he’s proven his quality and his ability on numerous occasions since joining City. Yes he’s not had the best couple of months but that’s the life of a goalkeeper. He’ll have experienced it before. He’ll experience it again. We shouldn’t forget all the brilliant stuff he does for the team.”.

#25623. What are fossil fuels?

What are fossil fuels?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life.
  • The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.
  • They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

Recent findings suggest that we transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

According to recent reports, fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Presently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

According to recent reports, three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete strategy, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres mentioned.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight newly introduced signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Industry observers note that everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

According to recent reports, the groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

According to recent reports, this is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. According to recent reports, newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Industry observers note that newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle stated. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”.

Recent findings suggest that everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

Sources indicate that “It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”.

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.

Ten-man Betis survive Navalcarnero scare at Santo Domingo as Riquelme wins it in extra time

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Football-espana

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real Betis needed a stoppage-time equaliser and extra time to beat Navalcarnero 3-2 in the Copa del Rey round of 128.
  • Industry observers note that real Betis came from behind late on to beat Navalcarnero in the Copa del Rey round of 128 on Thursday 12 November.
  • Industry observers note that the venue carried history for the Betis coach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real Betis needed a stoppage-time equaliser and extra time to beat Navalcarnero 3-2 in the Copa del Rey round of 128. Manuel Pellegrini's weakened side avoided an upset and now await the second-round draw.

Industry observers note that real Betis came from behind late on to beat Navalcarnero in the Copa del Rey round of 128 on Thursday 12 November. Riquelme settled the tie in extra time at Santo Domingo. Manuel Pellegrini’s side finished with ten men after Aitor Ruibal was sent off.

Industry observers note that the venue carried history for the Betis coach. Santo Domingo is where Pellegrini, then in charge of Real Madrid, suffered the 2009 cup defeat known as the ‘Alcorconazo’, El Gol Digital noted. Navalcarnero, founded in 1953, play in Group V of Segunda Federación. The club moved the tie away from its own Municipal Mariano González ground. It chose Santo Domingo, which holds roughly 5,000, to make room for its more than 2,000 members. The club remarked money was not the only reason.

Riquelme opened the scoring in the fifth minute from a Ruibal assist, and Betis led at half-time. Álvaro Leis equalised in the 49th minute from a free-kick routine set up by Navalcarnero’s coach. Leis then turned provider for K. Vazquez, who put the hosts ahead in the 79th minute.

Marina levelled in stoppage time, with Ruibal credited with the assist. Riquelme’s second goal came in the 96th minute. Diego Llorente went off in extra time after a heavy blow to the head. Isco missed a penalty in the 117th minute. Already booked in the 90+4th minute, Ruibal received a second yellow and a red card in the 118th. Navalcarnero felt they should have had a penalty for a challenge by Pablo Fornals, and the tie was played without VAR, Infobae (EFE) reported.

Industry observers note that the figures show how much Betis dominated. They had 73% of the ball, took 29 shots to Navalcarnero’s 12 and won 13 corners to 3. They completed 864 accurate passes. Dani Ceballos earned a 9.2 rating with 3 key passes. On the same night, Levante also needed extra time in the first round, winning 2-1 away to CD Tarancón.

Betis were without several regulars. Valles, Marc Roca, Abde, Parrott, Deossa and four other players were away on international duty. Cucho Hernández was injured. Betis agreed the newly introduced date after talks with the RFEF and Navalcarnero, knowing that any players called up by their national teams would miss the match.

The win follows a 2-0 victory over Elche. For Navalcarnero, the defeat ended a run of five matches without loss, including a 3-2 win over Numancia. They host Getafe II in Segunda División RFEF on Sunday 15 November. Betis visit Sevilla in LaLiga on Saturday 21 November.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shares in the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, in the biggest initial public offering of all time.Credit: Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty.
  • Industry observers note that anthropic, the frontier artificial-intelligence company, has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November.
  • It has been revealed that the maker of AI model Claude, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group who broke away from rival giant OpenAI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares in the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, in the biggest initial public offering of all time.Credit: Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty.

Industry observers note that anthropic, the frontier artificial-intelligence company, has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November. With a staggering valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, the firm, based in San Francisco, California, is now among the world’s most valuable companies — and it has major ambitions in science.

It has been revealed that the maker of AI model Claude, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group who broke away from rival giant OpenAI. Its models have proven powerful in research, and Anthropic has introduced its own directed science effort, focusing on areas including quantum mechanics and protein design. This year alone, it has reported mathematics breakthroughs and launched its first life sciences laboratory.

The IPO might also unleash a historic wave of philanthropy: all seven of Anthropic’s founders are likely to become billionaires and have pledged to donate 80% of their equity in the company to charity, including chief executive Dario Amodei. And on 18 October, the company revealed that it had established the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, created to support initiatives that benefit society and stocked with an initial commitment of 5% of Anthropic’s shares.

But the firm has drawn criticism from researchers, who say its aims of curing diseases on short timescales are unrealistic and that its race towards developing ultra-powerful, ‘superintelligent’ AI models pose serious risks, including an existential threat to humanity. In its public prospectus, published ahead of the IPO, Anthropic outlines a new governance structure that it says is “consistent with our commitment to AI safety and responsibility”, and adds that safety research directly shapes the firm’s “model design, training, and deployment.”.

Nature looks at four areas of science where Anthropic is making waves.

Industry observers note that AI’s potential to turbocharge the discovery of upcoming medicines has been a centerpiece of Anthropic’s pitch to investors. “If today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness — these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” Amodei noted in a promotional video ahead of the IPO.

According to recent reports, the firm has been rapidly expanding its biomedical ambitions. This year, Anthropic opened its first ‘wet’ laboratory for life sciences research, announced partnerships with several pharmaceutical companies, and remarked it was pursuing drug leads of its own. “We initiative to scale this work up substantially from here,” the company said on 27 October.

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

But Amodei’s habit of promising swift, AI-fueled cures for complex diseases has rankled many researchers and entrepreneurs in the field who feel the timeline is unrealistic.

Over the last year, Anthropic has made a major push in the life sciences. In June, the manufacturer hired John Jumper, who shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel Prize for his work on AlphaFold2 while at Google DeepMind in London.

It has been revealed that some of the company’s early biological research received a mixed reception from biologists. After Anthropic reported using a swarm of AI agents to find signs of a new CRISPR-like system in viral sequence data, some researchers questioned the novelty of the finding and noted that the company had not carried out the experimental work needed to determine the system’s function.

In a recent development, in protein design — a field that has boomed thanks to specialist AI tools including AlphaFold — Anthropic’s work has also failed to generate much excitement. In August, Anthropic used Claude Science — an agentic system that can access other biological tools and databases — to make novel ‘binders’ against 15 protein targets.

Industry observers note that “Expectations are sky high,” states Anthony Gitter, a computational biologist at the Morgridge Institute for Research in Madison, Wisconsin. “I understand why some view their initial public results as underwhelming.”.

In a recent development, but Gitter is enthusiastic about Anthropic’s protein design efforts, largely because the tech giant was transparent about the work, from the prompts it used to the sequences that were generated. “I would strongly encourage Anthropic to continue that in their future life sciences research,” Gitter adds.

In recent months, Anthropic and other companies — notably Google DeepMind and OpenAI — have been working to establish their research credentials in large part by showing off the rapidly growing mathematical abilities of their flagship AI models.

On 7 September Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and collaborator Tristan Buckmaster at New York University solved a special case of the Navier-Stokes equations, a long-standing problem in mathematical physics that describes the flow of fluids. Hours after Anthropic announced the result, OpenAI claimed a full solution of the problem, igniting a controversy.

In another collaboration, Alpöge and mathematical physicist Ethan Sussman at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, have been working towards establishing the mathematical foundations of the standard model of particle physics. This too is a problem on which OpenAI has made similar claims.

Anthropic and its competitors see the ability to write a rigorous proof of a mathematical fact as a crucial testing ground for their reasoning models. That’s in large part because the correctness of a proof is an objective measure that can be used as a ‘reward’ to further train AI systems.
